findings.title: Actor isolation is not guaranteed by the notification queue
findings.explanation: A `.main` OperationQueue does not establish Swift `MainActor` isolation, so `assumeIsolated` can trap when the callback runs without a MainActor executor; hop to the actor asynchronously instead.

findings.title: Persisted refresh interval can be outside the slider range
findings.explanation: Values loaded from UserDefaults are not validated or clamped to `15...300`, so an invalid stored value can leave the Slider with an unsupported selection and an inconsistent displayed interval.

findings.title: Validate persisted refresh intervals
findings.explanation: The value loaded from `UserDefaults` is accepted without enforcing the Stepper’s 60–3600 second range, so malformed or externally written values can leave the control out of range and non-finite or oversized values can trap when converted to `Int` in the label at line 136.

findings.title: Main-actor call from a Combine callback
findings.explanation: `receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)` guarantees runtime delivery on the main queue but does not establish `MainActor` isolation for the `sink` closure, so calling the actor-isolated `reloadFromDefaults()` can fail Swift 6 strict-concurrency checking; explicitly hop to `MainActor` in the callback.

findings.title: Timer survives view-model deallocation
findings.explanation: The run loop retains this repeating timer, and its weak capture means it will keep firing after the view model is released without invalidating itself; invalidate it when the stopwatch is torn down or otherwise tie the timer to the view model's lifecycle.

findings.title: Use a monotonic clock for elapsed time
findings.explanation: `Date` is wall-clock time and can jump when the system clock changes, causing the stopwatch to gain or lose time; measure intervals with a monotonic clock such as `ContinuousClock` instead.

findings.title: Lap and stop actions use a stale elapsed value
findings.explanation: `elapsed` is refreshed only by timer callbacks, so a lap or stop between callbacks records a value up to one timer interval old; compute the current elapsed duration synchronously when handling these actions.

findings.title: Accepts refresh intervals outside the picker options
findings.explanation: A stored or externally written interval that is not in `refreshIntervalOptions` is assigned directly, leaving the picker with no matching selection and potentially exposing an unusable setting.

findings.title: Stopping can discard elapsed time
findings.explanation: `elapsedTime` is only refreshed by timer callbacks, so stopping between ticks—or while the run loop is busy—stores a stale value and loses time since the last tick.

findings.title: Lap times use a stale stopwatch reading
findings.explanation: A lap records the last timer-updated `elapsedTime` rather than calculating the time at the lap action, so split and total times can lag by a tick or much longer if callbacks were delayed.

findings.title: Timer can outlive the view model
findings.explanation: The run loop retains the scheduled timer, and if the view model is released while running, its weak capture prevents a retain cycle but the timer continues firing indefinitely without anyone left to invalidate it.

findings.title: Default run-loop mode can pause display updates
findings.explanation: A timer scheduled in the default run-loop mode may stop firing during interactions that switch modes, such as scrolling, making the displayed time freeze until the interaction ends.

findings.title: Wall-clock changes affect stopwatch accuracy
findings.explanation: Using `Date` for elapsed-time measurement makes the stopwatch jump if the system clock is adjusted, so elapsed duration should be measured with a monotonic clock.

findings.title: Upload continuation can be resumed more than once
findings.explanation: `upload` has no one-shot completion guard, so repeated `onFinish` callbacks (or concurrent calls that overwrite the uploader callbacks) can resume a checked continuation more than once and trap.

findings.title: Upload cannot be cancelled
findings.explanation: The async wrapper does not connect task cancellation to the legacy upload or resume its continuation on cancellation, so a cancelled caller can remain suspended until the SDK eventually finishes.

findings.title: Concurrent uploads overwrite each other's callbacks
findings.explanation: `UploadBridge` shares one uploader and mutable callback properties, so overlapping `upload` calls replace each other's handlers and can leave a continuation suspended or deliver another upload's result.

findings.title: Progress stream is never finished on failure-free lifecycle end
findings.explanation: The stream is finished only by `onFinish`, with no deinitialization or cancellation cleanup; if the upload never calls its finish callback, consumers of `progressUpdates` can wait indefinitely.

findings.title: Geocoder continuation has no cancellation handling
findings.explanation: Cancelling a task while geocoding does not stop the legacy request or resume the continuation until its callback arrives, which can unnecessarily retain the suspended task.

findings.title: Old thumbnail remains when the URL changes
findings.explanation: The task resets `failed` but not `thumbnail`, so a cell can continue showing the previous URL's image and date while the new request loads or even after it fails.

findings.title: Cache grows without bound
findings.explanation: The shared cache retains every downloaded platform image indefinitely, so browsing many distinct URLs can cause substantial memory growth.

findings.title: Concurrent cache misses duplicate downloads
findings.explanation: The cache only stores completed entries, so simultaneous loads for the same uncached URL each start their own network request and can overwrite one another's result.

findings.title: Actor returns a potentially non-Sendable image across isolation
findings.explanation: `CachedThumbnail` contains a platform image, and returning it from an actor can violate Swift 6 concurrency checking on platforms where that image type is not `Sendable`.

findings.title: Cache grows without bound
findings.explanation: Every successfully downloaded full-resolution image is retained indefinitely, so scrolling through a large or changing URL set can cause substantial and sustained memory growth.

findings.title: HTTP error responses are not rejected
findings.explanation: `data(from:)` does not fail for HTTP error status codes, so the code may attempt to decode an error page as an image and report a misleading image-data failure instead of handling the response status.

findings.title: Progress stream is shared and permanently finished
findings.explanation: The stream is created once for the uploader, but every upload finishes its continuation, so a later upload emits no progress and concurrent uploads mix progress and can terminate the stream while another upload is active.

findings.title: Cancellation does not stop or unblock an upload
findings.explanation: If the calling task is cancelled, the legacy upload continues and the async call remains suspended until its callback arrives, because the continuation bridge has no cancellation handling or underlying-operation cancellation.

findings.title: Cached image crosses actor isolation without guaranteed Sendable conformance
findings.explanation: `thumbnail(for:)` returns `CachedThumbnail` across an actor boundary, but the type contains a platform image whose `Sendable` conformance is not guaranteed on all supported platforms, which can produce strict-concurrency errors or unsafe transfers.

findings.title: A cancelled load can overwrite state for a newer URL
findings.explanation: When `url` changes, the previous task may still complete or set `failed`, while `thumbnail` and `failed` are not reset, so an old result can be shown for the new URL or a cancelled request can leave the cell in a failed state.

findings.title: HTTP error responses are treated as successful downloads
findings.explanation: The response from `data(from:)` is discarded without checking for an `HTTPURLResponse` success status, so server errors can be handled as image data instead of reported as download failures.

findings.title: The shared cache retains every full-size image indefinitely
findings.explanation: The dictionary has no eviction or size limit and stores the downloaded images at their original resolution, so scrolling through many unique URLs can grow memory use without bound.

findings.title: Concurrent cells can download the same URL more than once
findings.explanation: The cache lookup and later insertion are separate operations, so cells requesting the same uncached URL concurrently can all start duplicate network requests.

findings.title: Geocoding ignores task cancellation
findings.explanation: The cancellation handler does nothing, so a cancelled caller remains suspended until the legacy callback completes and may receive a success result instead of cancellation.

findings.title: Progress stream is shared across uploads
findings.explanation: The stream is created once for the uploader and is finished when any upload completes, so later or concurrent uploads cannot reliably deliver their progress through it.

findings.title: Upload cancellation is ignored
findings.explanation: Cancelling the task neither aborts the legacy upload nor resumes the awaiting continuation, leaving the caller suspended until the upload eventually finishes.

findings.title: Cache retains every full-size image indefinitely
findings.explanation: The process-wide dictionary has no eviction or memory-pressure handling, so visiting many large images can grow memory usage without bound.

findings.title: Duplicate URLs produce duplicate view identities
findings.explanation: Because each cell is identified by its URL, repeated URLs in `urls` violate `ForEach`'s uniqueness requirement and can cause incorrect view reuse or runtime warnings.

findings.title: HTTP error responses are treated as image downloads
findings.explanation: `data(from:)` does not reject non-success HTTP status codes, so an error response containing image data can be cached and displayed as a valid thumbnail.

findings.title: Image decoding runs on the UI actor
findings.explanation: The SwiftUI task inherits the view's actor isolation, so constructing the platform image from potentially large data can block UI updates; decode or downsample off the main actor.

findings.title: Platform image crosses an actor boundary without Sendable guarantees
findings.explanation: `CachedThumbnail` contains `UIImage` or `NSImage` and is passed into and returned from `ThumbnailCache`; under strict Swift concurrency this non-Sendable value can produce isolation errors or unsafe cross-actor access.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff is reset on every socket attempt
findings.explanation: Resetting `reconnectDelay` in `openSocket()` means each failed connection schedules another retry after one second, so the intended exponential backoff never takes effect.

findings.title: Reconnect timers can open duplicate sockets
findings.explanation: Scheduled retries are not tracked or invalidated, so a retry from an earlier connection can still fire after `connect()` opens a new socket, and multiple failure callbacks can schedule multiple competing retries.

findings.title: Messages are silently discarded while disconnected
findings.explanation: If `task` is nil, or sending fails, the message is never queued or retried while `sendDraft()` still clears the draft, causing user messages to be lost.

findings.title: Repeated starts can create multiple socket connections
findings.explanation: `start()` always calls `connect()` without checking whether a socket or reconnect is already active, so repeated appearances can leave multiple receive loops running and duplicate incoming messages.

findings.title: Callbacks from old sockets can disrupt the current connection
findings.explanation: Receive and send callbacks do not verify that they belong to the current task, so a late failure from a canceled socket can cancel a newer connection or schedule another reconnect, including after a stop-and-start cycle.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff resets before a connection is established
findings.explanation: Resetting `reconnectDelay` immediately after resuming a socket means repeated connection failures always retry after one second instead of applying the intended exponential backoff.

findings.title: Drafts are discarded when no socket is available
findings.explanation: `sendDraft()` clears the draft after calling `send()`, but `send()` silently drops the message when encoding fails or `task` is nil, so a user can lose a message during a disconnect.

findings.title: Server echoes can create duplicate message identities
findings.explanation: The locally appended message and its server echo can share the same ID, leaving duplicate IDs in `messages` and violating `ForEach`'s identity requirement.

findings.title: Connection state is reported before the WebSocket connects
findings.explanation: `resume()` only starts the handshake, so setting `isConnected` here can make the UI report a connection even when the handshake subsequently fails.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff is reset on every connection attempt
findings.explanation: Resetting the attempt counter in `connect()` means each failed attempt schedules the same two-second delay, so the intended exponential backoff never takes effect.

findings.title: Callbacks from an obsolete socket can disconnect the current socket
findings.explanation: Disconnect handling does not check that the callback belongs to the current task, so a late receive or send failure from a cancelled connection can clear a newer connection and schedule an unnecessary reconnect.

findings.title: Pending reconnects can create duplicate connections after restart
findings.explanation: A reconnect task only checks `isStopped` when it wakes, so stopping and starting before its delay expires makes that stale task eligible to connect alongside the new connection.

findings.title: Receive loop continues after the connection is stopped
findings.explanation: A successful receive racing with `stop()` is handled and followed by another `listen(on:)` call without checking that the connection is still active, leaving a receive outstanding on a cancelled socket.

findings.title: Reconnect backoff is reset before the connection succeeds
findings.explanation: Resetting the delay on every connection attempt means repeated quick failures always reconnect after one second, so the configured exponential backoff never takes effect.

findings.title: Receive callbacks are not tied to the socket that started them
findings.explanation: A callback from an old socket can run after a reconnect and call `receiveNext()` on the new `webSocketTask`, creating overlapping receive loops and allowing stale failures to disrupt the active connection.

findings.title: Repeated starts can create multiple live sockets
findings.explanation: `start()` unconditionally creates a new connection, so repeated appearance or start calls can leave an earlier socket active and its callbacks can interfere with the current connection.

findings.title: Stale callbacks can mutate state after stop or restart
findings.explanation: Callbacks do not verify that their socket still belongs to the current connection, so a completion from a stopped connection can append messages or trigger reconnects after the view model has restarted.

findings.title: A stale send failure can tear down a newer connection
findings.explanation: The send completion schedules a reconnect without checking which socket failed, so a delayed failure from an old socket can clear and replace a healthy current connection.

findings.title: Failed sends silently lose the draft
findings.explanation: The message is appended and the draft is cleared before the send result is known, so a send failure leaves the message looking delivered while discarding the user's retryable text.

findings.title: Cancellation can be lost before continuation installation
findings.explanation: If cancellation runs before `box.set` installs the continuation, `resume` sees nothing and forgets the cancellation, so the operation can remain suspended forever if the legacy callback never arrives.

findings.title: Cancellation releases the upload slot while legacy work continues
findings.explanation: When the awaiting task is cancelled, the wrapper throws and clears `isUploading` even though the legacy upload is not stopped, allowing a second upload to start and its shared callbacks to be confused with the still-running first upload.

findings.title: Progress continuation access is unsynchronized
findings.explanation: Legacy callbacks may run on arbitrary queues while `progressContinuation` is replaced under `lock`, so reading and writing this property without the same synchronization creates a data race.

findings.title: Cancellation leaves the progress stream unfinished
findings.explanation: If the task is cancelled before `onFinish` fires, the wrapper exits without finishing `progressContinuation`, leaving stream consumers waiting indefinitely.

findings.title: Replacing the public progress stream makes observation timing-dependent
findings.explanation: A caller that reads `progressStream` before `upload` gets the initially finished stream, while each upload replaces the property, so clients can easily observe the wrong stream and concurrent reads are not synchronized.

findings.title: Progress buffering is unbounded
findings.explanation: `AsyncStream.makeStream()` uses an unbounded buffer by default, so a fast legacy producer and slow or absent consumer can accumulate progress events without limit.
